new_statements.quote: p. 70: "Mnogi kajkavski govori čuvaju još staru hrvatskosrpsku akcentuaciju sa 3 osnovna prahrvatskosrpska akcenta ̑ ̏ ̃, kako sam je ja već prije 25 godina uzimao (v. »Rad« 187, 207). Akcenat ̑ odgovara praslavenskom ̑ (u primjerima kao mȇso) i metatonijskom ̑ (u primjerima kao gen. pl. krȃvā); ̃ je po mome bilježenju t. zv. novi akut (u primjerima kao sũša); ̏ odgovara praslavenskom ̏ (u primjerima kao ȍko) i starom akutu (u primjerima kao krȁva)." — p. 73: "Konservativna grupa čuva više ili manje staru akcentuaciju, osobito mjesto starijega akcenta. U toj grupi možemo razlikovati dva pojasa, i to jedan s oksitonezom tipa ženȁ i drugi bez takve oksitoneze [...] Revolucionarna grupa karakterizirana je time, što se u njoj stara akcentuacija ne samo s obzirom na mjesto akcenta, nego i s obzirom na intonaciju više ili manje promijenila."
new_statements.translation: p. 70: "Many Kajkavian dialects still preserve the old Croato-Serbian accentuation with the 3 basic Proto-Croato-Serbian accents ̑ ̏ ̃, as I already assumed 25 years ago (see Rad 187, 207). The accent ̑ corresponds to Proto-Slavic ̑ (in examples like mȇso) and to the metatonic ̑ (in examples like gen. pl. krȃvā); ̃ is, in my notation, the so-called neo-acute (in examples like sũša); ̏ corresponds to Proto-Slavic ̏ (in examples like ȍko) and to the old acute (in examples like krȁva)." p. 73: "The conservative group preserves more or less the old accentuation, especially the place of the older accent. In this group we can distinguish two belts, one with oxytonesis of the type ženȁ and the other without such oxytonesis [...] The revolutionary group is characterised by the fact that in it the old accentuation has changed more or less not only with respect to the place of the accent but also with respect to intonation."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kajkavian has an empty rule; Ivšić supplies the substance: a free, lexically/morphologically placed three-tone pitch accent (ȁ ȃ ã) in the conservative dialects, with place shifts (metataxis) and tone changes (metatonia) in the eastern 'revolutionary' dialects and a weight-conditioned last-two-syllables rule in the Podravina subtype. Nothing in the catalog is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kajkavian has a three-way tonal accent system (short falling ȁ, long falling/circumflex ȃ, long rising 'neo-acute' ã) with contrastive intonation and quantity; the place of accent is not fixed to a syllable position but inherited lexically and morphologically (e.g. oxytone ženȁ vs. initial lȉpa, gen. pl. krȃvā vs. nom. krȁva, prez. mȋsli). Ivšić divides the dialects into a conservative group (old place of accent kept, with or without final-syllable oxytonesis of the žena type) and a revolutionary group (place shifted by 'metataxis' toward the word-beginning or word-end, and intonation changed by 'metatonia'), further split into four main groups (I older Kajkavian, II Čakavian-Kajkavian, III younger Kajkavian with metataxis, IV younger Kajkavian with metatonia), pp. 80-81.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 84 (p. 39): the Podravina type IV7-8 (Bregi, Novigrad, Virje, Đurđevec etc.) has a positional rule: "u njemu može biti akcentovan samo posljednji ili pretposljednji slog, i to posljednji, ako je iskonski ili sekundarno kajkavski dug, a pretposljednji, ako je posljednji kratak" — only the last or the penultimate syllable may be accented: the last if it is (originally or secondarily) long, otherwise the penult (e.g. mlȋnar, čȗvam, kravȃr, ženȁ > žȅna). Ivšić calls this the most 'revolutionary' type and states it derives from the common Kajkavian base, not from any Bulgarian parallel (p. 85). p. 74: educated Kajkavian speakers usually replace the neo-acute ã by the long falling accent (pȋšem, čȗvam).
new_statements.identity_note: Ivšić describes Croatian Kajkavian as a whole (the dialects of 'Hrvati kajkavci' north-west of the Štokavian line), with a four-group accentual classification: I older Kajkavian (Zagorje–Međimurje, west of a Delekovec–Krapina–Sv. Ivan Zelina line), II Čakavian-Kajkavian (Zaprešić–Sutla–Sava corner, western Samobor, Žumberak, the Sava–Bregana ikavian pocket), III younger Kajkavian with metataxis (Turopolje–Posavina, south-east), IV younger Kajkavian with metatonia (Križevci–Podravina, north-east). The weight-sensitive last-two-syllables rule (p. 84) is specific to the Podravina subtype IV7-8 (Bregi, Novigrad, Virje, Đurđevec). The ikavian Kajkavian speakers of Brdovec/Marija Gorica (§12, pp. 74-78) are said to have their own accentuation of Čakavian origin.

audit.recode_to: No category change (keep tonal-OR-pitch accent, lexical/mobile place, no secondary stress). Rewrite the primary-stress rule from Ivšić 1936 pp. 67-73: most Kajkavian dialects have a three-way accent system (short ȁ, long falling ȃ, neo-acute/long rising ã) with distinctive pitch and quantity, accent place lexically specified and paradigmatically mobile; sub-dialects differ by accent retraction/advancement (metataxis) and tone reversal (metatony), Virje-type Podravina dialects restrict the accent to the last two syllables; Rožić's Štokavian-style four-accent description applies only to the Prigorje border variety. Add caution that urban Zagreb Kajkavian is reported stress-only (Magner 1966, not yet read).
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and domain quote are verbatim in the held archive.org scanned of Rožić 1893-94 at the stated section (Rad 115 pp. 97-98; noun passages pp. 108-109). (2) Deciding source: a 192-pp. 1893-94 dialect monograph of a single border sub-dialect, analysed through the Štokavian four-accent template; Ivšić 1936 (downloaded now from HAZU DiZbi, open) re-quotes this exact passage and judges Rožić's short-accent notation confused, while stating that Kajkavian proper has three distinctive accents (ȁ ȃ ã) with free, paradigmatically mobile place and no Štokavian rising accents. That confirms the catalog category (pitch accent, lexical placement, no positional/weight rule, word domain) but shows the the primary-stress rule text over-generalises Rožić's Štokavian-style system to the languoid. (3) Better sources exist and are not yet obtained: Lončarić 1996 (standard monograph, print), Houtzagers 19
